title: K Closest Points to Origin
directAnswer: Rank points by squared distance x²+y² (skip the square root — it's monotonic and only adds floating-point error). The interview-grade answer is a max-heap of size k: push each point, pop when size exceeds k, and the k smallest distances survive — O(n log k) time, O(k) space. For O(n)-average time, mention quickselect to partition the k closest without ordering them.

remember.pattern: Size-k max-heap on squared distance (or quickselect)
rules: Compare **squared** distance `x²+y²`, never `sqrt` — sqrt is monotonic so ordering is identical, and it avoids float error and cost.
Use a **max-heap of size k** (largest distance on top) so the farthest of the current k is evicted when a closer point arrives.
Python's min-heap → **negate the distance** to get a max-heap.
The output order is unspecified — don't waste time sorting the final k unless asked.
If the interviewer wants O(n) average, switch to **quickselect** (partition around the k-th distance).
whenToUse: 'K closest / nearest / smallest by a computed key' problems
You need the k best by a metric without a full sort
Streaming points where k stays small relative to n
Any nearest-neighbour-style selection with a cheap distance proxy
antiSignals: k ≈ n → just sort all points by distance
You need them sorted by distance → sort directly, O(n log n)
k = 1 → linear scan for the single minimum
Need exact Euclidean distances for output → only then take sqrt at the end
remember.takeaway: K Closest is Top-K wearing a geometry costume: the only twist is the key (squared distance). A size-k max-heap gives O(n log k); quickselect gives O(n) average. Recognise it as the same bounded-heap pattern as Top K Frequent and Kth Largest.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you drop the square root (monotonicity insight), and whether you select with a size-k heap instead of sorting everything — plus awareness of quickselect for O(n) average.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Computing Math.sqrt for the comparison (slower and floating-point fragile), or using a min-heap of all n points and popping k — O(n log n) and O(n) memory.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Say 'compare squared distances' before writing code, give the heap O(n log k) solution, then offer quickselect O(n) average and discuss its worst case and why output order is free.

problemStatement:
Given an array `points` where `points[i] = [xᵢ, yᵢ]` represents a point on the X-Y plane and an integer `k`, return the `k` closest points to the origin `(0, 0)`.

The distance between two points is the Euclidean distance: √((x₁−x₂)² + (y₁−y₂)²). You may return the answer in **any order**. The answer is guaranteed to be unique (except for the order).
constraints: The answer is unique up to ordering
understanding: Select the k points nearest the origin. 'Nearest' is by Euclidean distance, but since we only compare distances, the squared distance x²+y² gives the identical ordering without any square roots. Output order doesn't matter.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does the output order matter?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No — any order is accepted. That's why a heap (partial order) or quickselect (no order) both work; no need to sort the final k.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can I compare squared distances instead of true distances?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. Square root is monotonic, so x²+y² preserves the ordering and avoids floating-point error and cost. I'll only sqrt if actual distances are required in the output.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Could two points tie in distance at the boundary?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The problem guarantees a unique answer set, so the cutoff is well-defined. If ties were allowed I'd confirm whether any valid set of k is acceptable.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How big is k relative to n?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: If k ≪ n, a size-k heap (O(n log k)) is great. If k ≈ n, just sort. Quickselect is O(n) average regardless of k.

Both squared distances are 1; k equals n so both points are returned.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach

approaches.name: Max-Heap of Size K
approaches.whenToMention: The default answer. Lead with 'compare squared distances and keep a heap of only the k closest seen so far'.
hints: You need the k smallest by a computed key. To keep 'the k best so far' while streaming, which heap orientation lets you evict the current worst?
Use a MAX-heap keyed by squared distance, capped at size k. The top is always the farthest of the k you're holding.
Push each point; if the heap exceeds k, pop the top (the farthest). After all points, the heap holds exactly the k closest.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each of n points triggers a push and possibly a pop, each O(log k) because the heap never exceeds k. Total O(n log k). The heap holds at most k entries → O(k) space.
approaches.explanation:
Treat it as Top-K with the key being squared distance.

**Why squared distance.** Euclidean distance is `√(x²+y²)`. Since `√` is strictly increasing, comparing `x²+y²` gives the *same ordering* as comparing the true distances — but with integer arithmetic, no precision loss, and no `sqrt` calls. Always state this; it's the cheapest way to look sharp.

**Why a max-heap of size k.** We want the k *smallest* distances. Counter-intuitively, keep a *max*-heap (farthest on top) capped at k. When a new point arrives and the heap is full, compare it implicitly: push it, then pop the top. The top is the farthest among the k+1 candidates, so popping it always discards the least deserving point. Whatever survives all n points is the k closest.

**Why not a min-heap of everything.** Heapifying all n points into a min-heap and popping k times is `O(n + k log n)` and stores all n. The size-k max-heap caps memory at k and each operation at `log k` — better when `k ≪ n`, and it generalises to streams where n is unbounded.

**Python detail.** `heapq` is a min-heap, so push `(-distance, x, y)`. The most-negative (largest true distance) sits on top and gets popped first — exactly the max-heap behaviour we want.
approaches.insight: The size-k max-heap is a bouncer keeping only the k closest in the club: the bouncer (heap top) is whoever is currently farthest, so any closer newcomer bumps them. You never compare points directly — the heap's ordering decides every eviction.

Negate distance so heapq's min-heap behaves as a max-heap on distance.

approaches.name: Quickselect (Optimal Average O(n))
approaches.whenToMention: Offer when asked to beat O(n log k) or for the best average time. It partitions the k closest without ordering them.
hints: You don't need the k closest sorted — you only need them grouped to the front. What algorithm partitions an array around a pivot so one side is 'smaller'?
Use quickselect (the selection cousin of quicksort): partition by squared distance so all distances ≤ pivot are on the left.
Recurse only into the side containing the boundary index k. Once the pivot lands at index k, the first k elements are the answer — in any order.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each partition is O(n) and quickselect recurses into only one side, so expected work is n + n/2 + n/4 + … = O(n). A pathological pivot sequence degrades to O(n²); randomising the pivot makes that astronomically unlikely.
approaches.explanation:
Quickselect finds the k smallest *without fully sorting*.

**Partition like quicksort, recurse like binary search.** Pick a pivot point, then rearrange so every point with squared distance ≤ the pivot's sits left of it and every farther point sits right. The pivot is now at its final sorted index `p`.

**Recurse into one side only.** If `p == k`, the first k slots hold exactly the k closest — done. If `p > k`, the answer is entirely within the left part, so recurse there. If `p < k`, the left part is fully in the answer; recurse right for the remaining `k − p`. Unlike quicksort, we discard the other half each time, which is why the expected cost collapses to linear.

**Why it can beat the heap.** No `log k` factor and no auxiliary heap — it rearranges in place. The cost is a worst case of `O(n²)` on adversarial pivots, mitigated by random pivot selection. Mention this trade: heap is `O(n log k)` guaranteed, quickselect is `O(n)` average but `O(n²)` worst.

**Output order is free.** Because we only need the k closest as a *set*, leaving them unsorted on the left is perfectly valid — that's what makes quickselect applicable here at all.
approaches.insight: Sorting answers 'what is the full order?' but the question only asks 'which k are smallest?'. Quickselect exploits that weaker requirement: it stops the instant the boundary is placed, never paying for order it doesn't need — the canonical 'selection, not sorting' optimization.

edgeCases.behavior: Quickselect drives the single minimum to index 0; return that one point.
Every comparison is ≤ pivot; partition still terminates and any k are valid.
Loop exits immediately (boundary trivially satisfied); return all points.

pitfalls: Recursing into BOTH sides — that's quicksort (O(n log n)), defeating the point of quickselect.
Off-by-one on the boundary (using p vs p+1) — return the wrong count of points.
Not randomising the pivot — sorted/adversarial input degrades to O(n²).

commonMistakes: Comparing actual Euclidean distances (Math.sqrt) instead of squared distances — slower and floating-point fragile.
Using a min-heap of all n points instead of a size-k max-heap — O(n log n) time and O(n) memory.
Sorting the final k points even though any order is accepted — wasted work.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Taking the square root unnecessarily
commonMistakesDetailed.why: sqrt is monotonic, so it never changes the ordering — it only adds cost and floating-point error that can mis-order near-ties.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
import math
d = math.sqrt(x * x + y * y)  # float, slower, can mis-tie
heapq.heappush(heap, (-d, x, y))
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
d = x * x + y * y  # integer squared distance, exact ordering
heapq.heappush(heap, (-d, x, y))

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Min-heap of all points instead of size-k max-heap
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Heapifying all n and popping k is O(n + k log n) and holds every point. A size-k max-heap is O(n log k) and O(k) memory — strictly better when k ≪ n.
